Although the contextual elements differ, real-life examples range from the domains of work (e.g., invest more effort today in learning new skills and becoming more productive to increase one's long-term salary, vs. postponing important tasks or continuing on autopilot with minimum effort), education (e.g., invest more effort in studying difficult subjects today to improve one's future grades and career opportunities, vs. study less deeply and choose simpler courses with the sole objective of passing), and health (e.g., exercising today to improve one's future health and life habits, vs. staying on the couch rewatching old TV shows). Crucially, the effort task models this basic trade-off in a way that enables us to study the choice to precommit, the role of trait self-control in this choice, and actual performance in all experimental conditions. Supporting external validity, Study 3 will explore the choice to pre-commit using scenario-based choices that are contextually closer to daily life, including the three different domains of work, education, and health.

Procedure

Participants were first asked to report gender, age and educational level, and then completed the 13-item brief self-control scale (Tangney et al., 2004; Cronbach's alpha reliability = .91), a 4-item mental fatigue scale (adapted from Sjåstad & Baumeister, 2018; Cronbach's alpha reliability = .89), and two filler items asking about general happiness and life satisfaction. Sample items for the trait self-control scale: "I am able to work effectively towards long-term goals", "People would say that I have very strong self-discipline", and "I have a hard time breaking bad habits" (reversed). Sample items for mental fatigue: "I feel tired right now", and "I feel exhausted right now". A complete list of all items from all measures across all our three studies is openly available at OSF: https://osf.io/karuw/?view_only=81f20dfeacdc4e90aa83dee6e1738be5.

After completing the background measures, participants were introduced to the matrixsolving task, which included one practice round consisting of three small matrixes and one practice round consisting of three large matrixes. After completing each practice round, participants answered four different questions related to the perceived effort and difficulty of the task: i) how many matrixes (out of three) they thought they solved correctly (0-3); ii) how difficult they thought the task was (7-point scale:1=not difficult at all,7=very difficult); iii) how effortful they thought the task was (7-point scale:1=not effortful at all,7=very effortful); and iv) the anticipated effort of solving 20 large (small) matrixes (7-point scale:1=no effort at all,7=very much effort). As validity evidence for our effort task, these items were included to assess whether participants in fact thought it required more mental effort to solve the large matrixes than the small matrixes, which is a basic premise in our study design.

Prior to the main part of the effort task, participants were then randomly assigned to one out of three experimental conditions in a between-subjects design. This part of the design was included to introduce controlled variation in the degree to which pre-commitment to the higheffort matrixes was optional, which enables a causal analysis of the effect of pre-commitment on subsequent performance. We will now describe each condition in turn.

1) No commitment:

Participants were asked to choose whether they wanted to solve a large or a small matrix before each trial, adding up to a series of 20 effort choices, in which they would receive a fixed reward of $.01 for each correctly solved large matrix. There was no economic reward for correctly solving the small matrixes ($.0). This condition served as a baseline control group, in which pre-commitment was not available in any form. It thus captures incentivized effort performance in the continuous presence of a non-incentivized low-effort option (small matrixes), which is typical of many real-world decisions between work and leisure.

2) Optional pre-commitment: Participants were asked whether they would like to have the option of choosing between the large and small matrix in each trial, or only be presented with the large matrix in each round. Hence, they were given the option to pre-commit in advance --that is, to remove the non-incentivized low-effort option from their future choice set and only be presented with the incentivized choice alternative. We included this condition for two reasons: (a) to identify the causal effect of optional pre-commitment on effort performance (as compared to the 'no commitment' control condition), and (b) to provide an initial test of whether the choice to pre-commit is positively correlated with individual differences in trait self-control.

3) Forced pre-commitment: Participants were only presented with the incentivized higheffort task in each trial. The forced pre-commitment condition is therefore analogous to a "paternalistic" policy, in which a regulator removes the low-effort/no-reward option from the choice environment of the individual to improve his or her welfare. This experimental condition was included to identify the pure causal effect of a pre-committed choice environment. Since participants in this group were only exposed to the incentivized effort task without a loweffort/no-reward alternative, there were no selection effects that would confound the relationship between voluntarily choosing to pre-commit and their performance. Importantly, it was still a free choice whether participants actually tried to solve each matrix, as opposed to waiting or doing something else, but if they wanted to solve the task their only choice option in each trial was an incentivized large matrix. Among the participants who were only exposed to the large matrixes in this forced pre-commitment condition, about 10% did not solve a single matrix, and among those who solved at least one large matrix there was considerable variation in how many such matrixes they solved. This suggests that people understood the voluntary nature of the task.

Results

Validity evidence: Perceived effort.

It is a basic premise of the current experimental design that the participants are making choices between a non-incentivized matrix-solving task requiring low effort versus a larger and incentivized version of the same task requiring high effort. Providing empirical validation of this premise, the self-reported measures following the practice round of the effort task confirmed that solving the large (vs. small) matrixes was indeed perceived as more difficult (M = 4.97, SD = 1.65 vs. M = 1.97, SD = 1.41, p < .001, d = 1.40) and requiring more effort (M = 5.65, SD = 1.46 vs. M = 3.53, SD = 1.86, p < .001, d = 1.07). In anticipation, the participants also thought that solving the large matrix in all 20 trials in the main part of the study would be more effortful than solving only the small matrixes (M = 6.11, SD = 1.26 vs. M = 4.46, SD = 1.83, p < .001, d = 0.93). Thus, the effort task was perceived the way it was intended by our participants.

The causal effect of pre-commitment. Figure 2 shows the mean number of correctly solved large matrixes across conditions in the main part of the study, a behavioral measure of effort performance, which is the primary dependent variable in Study 1.

The number of correctly solved large matrixes was lowest in the 'no commitment' control condition (M = 6.18, SD = 6.97), where the participants had to make continuous choices between the small and large matrix in each trial, without any chance to pre-commit. As predicted by our first hypothesis in the pre-registration (H1), the number of correctly solved large matrixes increased when participants were given the option to pre-commit to only be presented with large matrixes (M = 7.82, SD = 7.37). In line with our second hypothesis (H2), the number of correctly solved large matrixes increased even further in the paternalistic condition of forced precommitment (M = 10.61, SD = 7.00), in which the non-incentivized low-effort matrixes were removed for all participants in advance.

The treatment differences between the three conditions are statistically significant at the pre-specified alpha level (p < .05, two-tailed), with the following effect sizes for each group comparison: no commitment < optional pre-commitment (d = .22, 95% CI [.08, .37], p = .003), optional pre-commitment < forced pre-commitment (d = .38, 95% CI [.23, .53], p < .001), and no commitment < forced pre-commitment (d = .60, 95% CI [.46, .75], p < .001). A visual inspection of the effect sizes shows that offering optional pre-commitment had a moderate but significant effect on effort performance, whereas the effect of the paternalistic policy condition (forced precommitment) on effort performance was almost three times as large. Participants who were given the option to pre-commit ('optional pre-commit') or randomly assigned to a paternalistic policy condition ('forced pre-commit') performed significantly better at the behavioral effort task than participants who had to continuously choose between the non-incentivized small matrix and the incentivized large matrix in each trial ("no commitment") (p-values < .003 -.001, d-values = .22 -.60).

Number of attempts.

As a non-registered explorative analysis to shed further light on why pre-commitment increased effort performance, we found that 'optional pre-commitment' caused an increase in the number of attempts to solve the large matrix relative to the 'no commitment' condition (M = 14.12, SD = 8.51 vs. M = 10.01, SD = 8.29, p < .001, d = 0.48). This finding is illustrated in Figure 3. The proportion of people choosing to only try to solve large matrixes increased from 25% in the 'no commitment' condition to 62% in the 'optional pre-commitment' condition (p < .001), and this change was due to fewer participants switching back and forth between solving large and small matrixes. This result suggests that the small matrix is indeed a tempting distraction when present (although solving it generates no extra payment), and that the option to pre-commit helped some participants to avoid that temptation pre-emptively, which was ultimately associated with better effort performance and higher earnings than in the control group (i.e., higher number of correctly solved large matrixes). All participants in all conditions were free to simply wait through each trial if they wanted to. Participants who were given the option to pre-commit to the incentivized high-effort option, or were forced to do so in a paternalistic policy condition, were significantly more likely to try to solve the maximum amount of 20 large matrixes (p < .001).

Trait self-control and the choice to pre-commit. Of the 336 participants randomly assigned to the optional pre-commitment condition, 198 (59%) freely chose to pre-commit, and participants who chose to pre-commit solved significantly more large matrixes (M = 11.11, SD = 6.86) than participants who did not (M = 3.09, SD = 5.22). In Study 1, however, we did not find support for our third hypothesis, which predicted that trait self-control would be positively correlated with the choice to pre-commit at p < .05 (r = .049, 95% CI [-.06, .15], p = .368).

When exploring this result in some more depth, we note that the proportion choosing to pre-commit is 52% among participants with low trait self-control (1SD below the mean), and 61% for participants with medium (+/-1SD from the mean) and high self-control (1SD above the mean), although the difference between these groups, equivalent to 9 percentage points and a Cohen's d of 0.2, is not statistically significant (p = .178) with the available sample size in Study 1.

Based on these indicative results from Study 1, we reasoned that a larger sample would be needed to test the Ulyssean self-control hypothesis with greater precision. Specifically, we conducted Study 2 with a considerably larger sample size for this trait-level analysis, which should provide sufficient statistical power to detect an effect of the same magnitude as the nonsignificant correlation we observed in our first study, if there should be a true and robust effect of this kind. Based on Study 1 alone, we found clear evidence for a positive causal effect of precommitment, while there was no robust evidence for the Ulyssean self-control hypothesis.

As a final non-registered explorative analysis from Study 1, we note that trait self-control was positively correlated with performance on the matrix-solving task in the no commitment condition (i.e., when pre-commitment was unavailable), controlling for practice trial performance (B = 0.774, p = .010). This result should be treated with caution due to the exploratory nature and small sample size, but in addition to the central importance of avoiding temptation by pre-commitment (main hypothesis in Studies 2 and 3), it suggests that people with high trait selfcontrol might also be better at resisting temptation in behavioral performance tasks.

Study 2: Participants With Low Trait Self-Control Avoid Pre-Commitment

In our second experiment, we conducted a similar type of online study as Study 1, but this time we gave all participants the option to pre-commit. Since the causal effect of pre-commitment was documented clearly in Study 1, the new design of Study 2 enables a more focused, high-powered test of the Ulyssean self-control hypothesis -namely, that self-control as a general trait is positively and significantly correlated with the choice to pre-commit. As a second addition, Study 2 includes a novel information treatment to examine whether knowledge about the performance benefits of pre-commitment would lead to higher pre-commitment rates, both for participants with high and low self-control.

Method

In Study 2, we recruited 1,121 participants from Amazon Mechanical Turk, and the final sample used in the analysis includes the 1,010 individuals (406 female, mean age = 37) who completed the study (which was balanced across treatment conditions).

According to our power analysis in STATA, the final sample of Study 2 provides an 80% chance of detecting a simple main effect of the information treatment corresponding to a Cohen's d = .18 or larger in an independent t-test (p < .05, two-tailed). When focusing on the correlational analysis of trait self-control and the choice to pre-commit, the final sample provides an 80% chance to detect a correlation coefficient of r = .09 or larger (p < .05, two-tailed) and a difference in pre-commitment choice of 9 percentage points or larger when comparing people with low versus medium/high trait self-control (p < .05, two-tailed). This means that Study 2 had sufficient power to reliably detect a wider range of effect sizes than Study 1. The hypotheses, method and statistical analysis were pre-registered in advance of the data collection, on the 27 th of November 2019: https://aspredicted.org/wwdj-szd4.pdf.

Procedure

The background questions, trait self-control measure, and the trial rounds of the effort task were identical to Study 1 and placed before the choice to pre-commit. After that, participants in Study 2 were randomly assigned to either receive information about the performance benefits of precommitment (Information) or not (Control). Thus, it was a between-subjects design with two conditions.

The text in the information condition was the following: "For your information: In a previous study, we found that people who only were presented with a large matrix in each of the 20 trials solved almost twice as many large matrixes than people who could choose freely between solving either large or small matrixes in each of the 20 trials. As a result, the participants who were only presented with the large matrixes earned a bonus that was twice as high." As can be seen from the results from Study 1, this information message was truthful and accurate.

On the next screen, participants in both conditions were asked to state in which case (A or B) they thought they would solve the greatest number of large matrixes:

A) If you are allowed to choose freely between solving either the large or the small matrix in each of the 20 trials. B) If you are only presented with the large matrix in each of the 20 trials.

The answer to this question was given on a response scale from 1-7, where 1 corresponded to "Definitely A", 4 corresponded to "No difference", and 7 corresponded to "Definitely B". This item was included to elicit subjective beliefs about the expected performance benefits of precommitment, and to what extent a possible change in beliefs should occur after the information treatment. Finally, all participants made a real choice of whether they would like to pre-commit to the high-effort/high-reward task only (large matrixes) or not, and then continued to the matrixsolving task in accordance with their preference. Because all participants in Study 2 were provided a free choice to pre-commit, the Ulyssean self-control hypothesis could be tested with much higher statistical power since the full sample could be used in that analysis. In contrast, only one out of three conditions in Study 1 could be used in the test of that hypothesis.

Results

Validity evidence: Perceived effort.

Mirroring the results from Study 1, the self-reported measures following the practice round of the effort task in Study 2 confirmed that solving the large (vs. small) matrixes was perceived as more difficult (M = 4.97, SD = 1.64 vs. M = 2.56, SD = 1.90, p < .001, d = 1.13) and requiring more effort (M = 5.72, SD = 1.40 vs. M = 3.93, SD = 1.96, p < .001, d = 0.93). In anticipation, solving the large matrix in all 20 trials in the main part of the study was also perceived as more effortful than solving only the small matrixes (M = 6.12, SD = 1.24 vs. M = 4.73, SD = 1.82, p < .001, d = 0.81).

Trait self-control and the choice to pre-commit. Consistent with our first hypothesis in this study (H1), the positive correlation between trait self-control and the choice to pre-commit was statistically significant (r = .25, 95% CI [.19, .31], p < .001). As can be seen from Figure 4, the proportion choosing to pre-commit is 23% for participants with low trait self-control (1SD below the mean), 50% for people with medium (average) self-control, and 58% among people with high trait self-control (1SD above the mean). Thus, the difference in pre-commitment choice between high and low trait self-control corresponds to 35 percentage points. Moreover, all internal differences between these three groups are statistically different from each other at the 5% alpha level (two-tailed), providing evidence that the positive correlation between trait self-control and the choice to pre-commit is present both when moving from low to medium and from medium to high self-control.

These results provide robust support for the Ulyssean self-control hypothesis in a highpowered test, which predicts that pre-commitment is effective in promoting effort performance, but that choosing this strategy freely relies on pre-existing levels of good self-control.

In an exploratory analysis, we observed a similar pattern for state-level self-control, as indicated by an initial measure of mental fatigue. Specifically, we found a negative and statistically significant correlation between the momentary feeling of being tired and exhausted across the four fatigue items and the choice to pre-commit to the incentivized high-effort task (r = -.25, p < .001), which suggests that the willingness to use pre-commitment strategies may also vary within individuals over time. That said, the positive correlation between trait self-control and the choice to pre-commit was robust to the inclusion of mental fatigue as a control variable (r = .13, p < .001). The causal effect of information on the choice to pre-commit. Among the 1,010 participants in Study 2, 469 (46%) decided to pre-commit. As predicted by our second hypothesis (H2)foot_0 , a t-test confirmed that information about the performance benefits of pre-commitment increased the proportion that chose to pre-commit from 41.2% in the control condition to 51.8% in the information condition (d = .22, 95% CI [.10, .34], p < .001). That is, participants who were provided information about the performance benefits of pre-committing were more likely to pre-commit than participants who did not receive this information in the control condition. The results for both main hypotheses were robust and reached the same conclusion when analyzed with chi-square tests instead of the pre-registered t-tests.

Explorative analysis. Further inspection of the results provided no support for the possibility that participants with low trait self-control responded differently to the information treatment than participants with high self-control, as the interaction effect is close to zero and far from statistically significant both for the choice to pre-commit (p = .881) and for subjective beliefs about the effect of pre-commitment (p = .689). This suggests that receiving information about the effectiveness of pre-commitment has an average positive effect on choosing pre-commitment, but does not reduce the gap in pre-commitment choice between people with high vs. low trait selfcontrol.

Turning to the role of pre-commitment in explaining performance differences between people with varying levels of self-control, we note that trait self-control is highly correlated with the number of large matrixes solved, controlling for trial round performance (Table 1, column 1), but when we include the choice to pre-commit as a control variable the point estimate shrinks by 71 percent. That is, participants with high trait self-control were more likely to perform well in the behavioral effort task, but an important part of the explanation appears to be that participants with high self-control are much more likely to choose the pre-commitment strategy than participants with low self-control.

The role of beliefs. Continuing our secondary analyses, we will end with an examination of the role of performance beliefs as a possible mechanism underlying the causal effect of the information treatment. Providing information about the performance benefits can influence precommitment choice for several reasons. One possibility is that people are misinformed about the performance benefits, in which case correcting these beliefs with new information could then increase the proportion choosing to pre-commit.

Figure 5 shows the distribution of answers to the belief question in the control and information conditions. The first thing to note is that the majority of people in both groups think that pre-commitment will increase performance on the incentivized large matrixes, although a substantial proportion (about 25%) believe that they will solve more large matrixes without precommitment. Second, there is a certain tendency that the information treatment shifts the distribution to the right (i.e., in favor of pre-commitment), but a Mann-Whitney test of a difference in distributions only found a suggestive but non-significant effect (p = .079), which was also true for a t-test of the difference in means between the two conditions (M = 4.66, SD = 2.23 vs. M = 4.91, SD = 2.11, p = .064). Hence, the information treatment seemed to have a relatively minor impact on the beliefs of subjects, which implies that the effect of information on precommitment choice is likely to be attributed to a broader set of factors than a change in their efficacy beliefs alone. Other possible explanations of the underlying mechanism of the information treatment remain to be studied in future research. For now, we conclude that the causal effect of providing efficacy information was modest but statistically significant, and that it was about equally effective for participants with high and low self-control as a general trait. At least based on these results, it seems unlikely that the avoidance of pre-commitment is driven by incorrect beliefs about specific performance benefits, but instead, a lower tendency to make strategic choices about one's future work environment that is consistent with this understanding. In addition to providing a conceptual replication of the positive link between trait self-control and pre-commitment choice, Study 3 will also explore a broader set of potential processes involved in the general tendency to choose precommitment strategies in goal pursuit.

Study 3: Ulyssean Self-Control Across Three Life Domains

Studies 1 and 2 tested the Ulyssean self-control hypothesis with a behavioral effort task in a controlled online environment. This approach provided high internal validity and an incentivized measure of actual performance, which is rarely done in self-regulation and goal pursuit research. However, it leaves open the question of external validity: Will the positive link between trait selfcontrol and pre-commitment choice generalize to different goal domains, closer to daily life? In addition, Studies 1 and 2 also had limited focus on the psychological processes related to precommitment choice, as they focused mostly on establishing the causal performance effect of precommitment, and the general role of trait self-control in pre-commitment choice.

In Study 3, we therefore tested the same overarching hypothesis, Ulyssean self-control, with two important additions. First, participants were asked to consider a set of four precommitment strategies to reach a long-term goal, situated in three different life domains: health, work, and education. This enables a test of whether trait self-control is positively associated with a broader tendency to choose pre-commitment strategies across different life domains. Second, to better understand why people with high self-control might be more likely to use pre-commitment strategies, we explored three different reasons to pre-commit as potential process mechanisms: A stronger temporal focus on future goal achievement, greater prior familiarity with commitment strategies, and considering pre-commitment a smart way to avoid temptations and distractions.

Our primary hypothesis (H1) was that trait self-control would be positively correlated with the average likelihood of choosing pre-commitment across the three domains. As secondary hypotheses, we predicted that trait self-control would be positively correlated with each of the three reasons to pre-commit (H2a-c), and that the three reasons would in turn be positively associated with pre-commitment choice and would jointly mediate the association between trait self-control and pre-commitment choice (H3). In addition, we explored whether the data would be consistent with a serial mediation model (Hayes, 2022), in which future focus and strategy familiarity represent a first stage in the decision process, which feeds into temptation avoidance as a second stage, before the choice to pre-commit. To be sure, this type of observational mediation analysis on correlational data does not warrant causal inference, as it typically rests on strong assumptions of no reverse causality or confounding third variables. Moreover, it cannot be used to exclude other potential model alternatives that remain possible. Instead, this approach may provide suggestive evidence of whether the observed data are consistent with our proposed model of the process connecting trait self-control with pre-commitment choice, which was preregistered as an exploratory analysis.

Method

In Study 3, we recruited U.S. participants from Prolific with a pre-registered target sample of 1,050. All participants who completed the full survey were included in the analysis, resulting in a final sample of 1,037 individuals (560 female, 466 male, 11 non-binary or not reported; mean age = 44.3, SD = 14.5). There were no further exclusions. According to a sensitivity power analysis, the final sample provided an 80% chance of detecting a correlation coefficient of r = .09 or larger (p < .05, two-tailed). Median completion time was 4.5 minutes. The hypotheses, method, and statistical analyses were pre-registered in advance of the data collection, on the 1 st of October 2026: https://aspredicted.org/me4t3e.pdf.

Procedure

Participants first reported their age, gender, income, and educational level, and then completed the same 13-item brief self-control scale as in Studies 1 and 2 (Tangney et al., 2004; Cronbach's alpha reliability = .90), a 5-item mental fatigue scale (Cronbach's alpha reliability = .87), and the two filler items asking about general happiness and life satisfaction.

Participants were then presented with three brief choice scenarios, one at a time and in randomized order, each describing and asking the participants to imagine an overarching goal they wanted to achieve in a different life domain: improving one's diet and getting regular exercise every week over the next eight weeks (health), becoming more productive by doing more and better work per day over the next eight weeks (work), and being a student who would move on to graduate on time with top grades (education). After reading each scenario, participants indicated how likely they would be to choose each of four commitment strategies, adapted to each goal domain, on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely,7 = very likely). Using sample items from the health domain, the four strategies were briefly described as the following: 1) "Sign up for an 8-week exercise program with scheduled sessions every week, in which you must message the instructor if you should not be able to attend a planned training session", 2) "Block off specific parts of the day in your calendar each week that you want to dedicate to exercise, so that no appointments or other interruptions can take place during those times", 3) "Set a clear exercise goal for what you want to achieve during the coming eight weeks, and then share this goal with someone that can hold you accountable by asking whether you succeeded in the end", and 4) "Set a clear exercise goal in your calendar for how much you want to have achieved at the end of each week, so you can monitor your progress along the way and make sure you are on track to reach your main goal in eight weeks". The logic of the commitment strategies was the same across the three domains, but small changes were made to adapt them to each domain (e.g., commitment strategy number two for the work domain: "Block off specific parts of the day in your calendar each week that you want to dedicate to focused work on your most important and challenging tasks, so that no appointments or other interruptions can take place during those times").

The strategies combine different aspects of pre-commitment, including blocking goalinconsistent options from one's future choice environment, increasing the future cost of deviating from one's goal, automatizing explicit self-monitoring towards the goal, and social commitment. In line with the pre-registration, the primary dependent variable was the average likelihood of choosing pre-commitment strategies across all 12 items from the three domains. The internal reliability of the general pre-commitment index was very good (Cronbach's alpha reliability = .86), which is the basis for testing our main hypothesis. The reliability of the three 4-item subscales was lower and somewhat below the conventional .7 benchmark in scale validation work (work = .64, education = .67, health = .67). In the current context we consider the subscale reliability as moderate but sufficient for exploratory analyses of broad group-level comparisons in average precommitment choice, given the short nature of the subscale (which is associated with lower Cronbach's alpha estimates).

Following the pre-commitment choices in the three different domains, participants rated to what extent they had generally focused on three potential reasons when making their choices of using the commitment strategies, on a 7-point scale (1 = not at all,7 = very much). The specific items were as follows: future focus ("I focused on what I want to achieve in the future"), strategy familiarity ("I focused on following a strategy I am used to, and such commitment strategies are familiar to me"), and temptation avoidance ("I thought the commitment strategies seemed like a smart way to avoid distractions and temptations").

Results

Descriptive statistics and intercorrelations for all primary study variables are presented in Table 2. In the text below, we first review the results for the primary hypothesis test, followed by an exploration of potential process mechanisms. Trait self-control and the choice to pre-commit. Consistent with our primary pre-registered hypothesis (H1), the results reveal that the correlation between trait self-control and the average likelihood of choosing pre-commitment strategies across the three life domains was positive and statistically significant, r(1035) = .27, 95% CI [.21, .33], p < .001. A domain-specific explorative analysis shows that this positive correlation was also present within each of the three life domains: health, r = .25, 95% CI [.19, .31]; work, r = .22, 95% CI [.16, .27]; and education, r = .25, 95% CI [.20, .31] (all ps < .001). At the level of individual commitment strategies, all 12 correlations with trait self-control were directionally consistent in the positive direction and statistically significant, although they varied in size (rs = .08 to .25, all ps ≤ .007, Holm-corrected). Thus, both across and within three different life domains, people with high trait self-control were more likely to choose pre-commitment strategies than people with low trait self-control.

Mirroring the exploratory analysis in Study 2, the momentary feeling of mental fatigue was negatively correlated with the likelihood of choosing pre-commitment, r = -.13, p < .001. This suggests that pre-commitment choice might also vary as a function of within-person variation in self-control capacity versus mental fatigue over time. However, the coefficient for trait self-control as an individual difference was about twice as large as the coefficient for mental fatigue, and like Study 2, the positive correlation between trait self-control and pre-commitment choice in Study 3 was robust to the inclusion of mental fatigue as a control variable (partial r = .24, p < .001).

Trait self-control and reasons to pre-commit. As predicted by our secondary hypotheses in the pre-registration, trait self-control was positively correlated with all three potential reasons to pre-commit, although the size of the associations varied somewhat: future focus (H2a), r = .31, 95% CI [.25, .36]; strategy familiarity (H2b), r = .22, 95% CI [.16, .28]; and temptation avoidance (H2c), r = .17, 95% CI [.11, .23] (all ps < .001). In turn, each of these three reasons was also positively correlated with the likelihood of choosing pre-commitment, with again some variations in size (rs = .30 to .54, all ps < .001). See Table 2 for an overview of all raw correlations between the primary study variables.

Mediation analysis.

To test to what extent these different reasons to pre-commit jointly could account for the positive association between trait self-control and pre-commitment choice (H3), we estimated a mediation model with all three variables as mediators, using ordinary least squares regression on z-standardized variables and percentile bootstrap 95% confidence intervals based on 10,000 resamples. Consistent with this general and pre-registered mediation hypothesis, the total indirect effect was positive and statistically significant, ab = .15, 95% CI [.11, .20], accounting for 57% (95% CI [44%, 73%]) of the total effect of trait self-control on pre-commitment choice. The direct effect of trait self-control remained significant after accounting for the three mediators, β = .12, 95% CI [.06, .17], p < .001, indicating partial mediation. In the most general sense, this mediation analysis suggests that the tendency for people with high (vs. low) trait selfcontrol to choose pre-commitment more often is related to a systematic tendency for these individuals to rely more on all three of these reasons to choose pre-commitment strategies: focus on future goal achievement, strategy familiarity, and temptation avoidance.

When considering each mediator individually, using a parallel mediation model that in practice treats the three mediators as competing explanations by estimating each mediator's association with pre-commitment choice while controlling for the other two mediators, the indirect effects through future focus, ab = .07, 95% CI [.05, .10], and temptation avoidance, ab = .07, 95% CI [.04, .10], were significant, whereas the indirect effect through strategy familiarity was not, ab = .01, 95% CI [-.00, .03]. The results of this model suggest that when considered in isolation, future focus and temptation avoidance were the most powerful mediators, and that strategy familiarity no longer mediated the main effect on its own when controlling for these other two pathways.

As a pre-registered exploratory analysis, we then examined whether the data were consistent with a serial mediation model (PROCESS Model 80; Hayes, 2022), in which future focus and strategy familiarity were treated as parallel first-stage mediators, feeding into temptation avoidance as the second mediator stage, before pre-commitment choice as the outcome variable (Figure 6). Informed by the broader idea of Ulyssean self-control, we consider this to be an interesting analysis as it theoretically proposes that the tendency for people with high (vs. low) trait self-control to use pre-commitment strategies more often operates through a combination of habits (strategy familiarity) and future-oriented temporal focus, which in turn is associated with a stronger strategic focus on avoiding temptations and distractions when pre-commitment choices are made.

Consistent with this reasoning, as illustrated in Figure 6, the results from the serial mediation analysis found that participants with high (vs. low) trait self-control reported a stronger focus on future goal achievement (β = .31) and strategy familiarity (β = .22), both of which positively predicted temptation avoidance (β = .40 and β = .17, respectively), which in turn was the strongest predictor of pre-commitment choice (β = .39; all ps < .001). Accordingly, both serial indirect effects were statistically significant: via future focus and temptation avoidance, ab = .05, 95% CI [.03, .06], and via strategy familiarity and temptation avoidance, ab = .01, 95% CI [.01, .03]. Future focus also had a significant direct link to pre-commitment choice, β = .24, p < .001, producing an additional indirect effect, ab = .07, 95% CI [.05, .10]. In contrast, trait self-control did not predict temptation avoidance once future focus and familiarity were accounted for, β = .01, p = .720, so the association between trait self-control and temptation avoidance was fully accounted for by the first-stage mediators. This analysis focused on the average tendency to pre-commit across the three life domains. As a non-registered explorative analysis, we found that both serial indirect effects were also significant within each of the three life domains, with highly similar estimates (via future focus: abs = .04; via familiarity: abs = .01), and the total indirect effect was also significant in all three domains (health: ab = .13, 95% CI [.09, .17]; work: ab = .13, 95% CI [.09, .17]; education: ab = .15, 95% CI [.11, .19]). For a complete overview of all estimates for all included variables in both the parallel and serial mediation models, please see Table 1 in the online appendix at OSF (https://osf.io/karuw/?view_only=81f20dfeacdc4e90aa83dee6e1738be5). Seen as a whole, the results of Study 3 extend the Ulyssean self-control hypothesis from a controlled effort task to everyday goal pursuit in three central life domains. In scenario-based choice scenarios across health, work, and education, people with high trait self-control were more likely to choose pre-commitment strategies to reach their goals. As a second contribution from Study 3, we found that more than half of this positive association was statistically accounted for by the reasons that participants reported for their choices, including future focus, strategy familiarity, and temptation avoidance. Because the mediators were measured after the pre-commitment choice and the study design is observational, these correlational results are consistent with the proposed theoretical mechanisms but do not establish a causal relationship or their temporal ordering. Alternative models remain possible. For a complete overview of all pre-registered Discussion Pre-commitment is often presented as an evidence-based solution to self-control problems. Consistent with this advice, the current research provides causal evidence that precommitment strategies can be highly effective at promoting effort performance. On average, both optional and "paternalistic" pre-commitment led to better performance and higher earnings than offering no commitment.

As our main contribution, we also studied who are most and least likely to select the pre-commitment strategy when it is offered as a free choice. Study 1 identified a suggestive but non-significant positive relationship between trait self-control and pre-commitment choice, corresponding to a choice difference of 9 percentage points. To enable a more reliable test, the sample size of Study 2 was three times larger than the free-choice condition in Study 1. These results revealed that people who are already successful at regulating their behavior, as indicated by high self-control as a general trait, were 35 percentage points more likely to choose the pre-commitment strategy than people with low self-control. In turn, participants with high self-control in Study 2 also performed better and earned more money than participants with low self-control. These findings were statistically significant and highly robust, suggesting that those who struggle with frequent self-control problems and perhaps could benefit the most from pre-commitment strategies are also the least likely to make use of them.

Supporting external validity, Study 3 provided a high-powered conceptual replication of the positive link between trait self-control and pre-commitment in scenario-based choice, finding that people with high (vs. low) trait self-control were more likely to choose precommitment strategies across all three life domains included in the study: health, work, and education. In addition, Study 3 also provided suggestive evidence for potential process mechanisms, as a mediation analysis found that 57% of the positive association between trait self-control and pre-commitment choice could be accounted for by a related tendency for people with high trait self-control to express higher levels of future goal focus, strategy familiarity, and temptation avoidance. These are the main findings across a series of three pre-registered studies and a total sample of 3,059 participants.

Implications for Psychology and Public Policy

The findings are consistent with our notion of Ulyssean self-control: Pre-commitment is highly effective, but choosing it freely requires good self-control. This is a theoretical and empirical extension of a larger trend in the last decade or so, in which the emphasis has shifted from pure self-restraint to strategic planning and temptation avoidance in understanding good self-control (Ent et al., 2015; Hofmann et al., 2012; Lopez et al., 2021). It adds to this literature by focusing specifically on pre-commitment choice, and by assessing incentivized behavioral performance, not just self-reported outcomes. It also contributes to the initial focus in early self-control research on specific regulation strategies, seeking to better understand the relationship between individual traits and flexible interaction with the environment (Mischel, 1974 (Mischel, , 2014)). The current research highlights the importance of what kind of choice environment the person navigates towards in the first place, not just what the person does once she arrives. People can use their self-control to reduce their future choice set and in other ways create a goal-consistent choice environment, thereby making it easier to perform well.

At the individual level, pre-commitment can be a wonderful tool to reach one's goals and change one's behavior for the better. It might also be one part of the explanation for why people with good self-control are more likely to enjoy positive life outcomes. At the societal level, however, offering optional pre-commitment devices appears to be an unlikely solution for those who would need it the most, and might even amplify existing performance inequalities due to unequal take-up. If it is a normative policy goal to reduce large societal inequalities and reach those who need it the most, the current research suggests that structural interventions changing the choice environment rather than the individual decision-maker will be most effective.

As limits of generalizability, we note that all three studies in the current paper were conducted in an online setting, with participants from only one country (USA), and only two different types of study designs. To what extent the findings will generalize to a wider range of cultural settings, and different methods than controlled effort experiments and surveybased choices, is therefore an important question for future research. In addition to experimentally varying the pure effort level between choice alternatives, it would also be interesting to see future work examining the role of more intensely gratifying temptations or leisurely low-effort options, when people are faced with the decision to pre-commit.

For now, we conclude that the current research has provided causal evidence for the effectiveness of pre-commitment on incentivized effort performance, but also revealed that those who could need it the most are the least likely to choose this pre-commitment strategy when it is optional: Individuals with low trait self-control.

Example of an effort choice between a small (a) and large (b) matrix, in which a correctly solved matrix generated an economic reward only for the large matrix (b). The effort task consists of 20 trials, in which only the large matrixes were presented in the pre-commitment version. The time duration was fixed at 50 seconds per trial, and it was voluntary to actually solve the matrix in all conditions.

Figure 2 :

Figure 2: Study 1 (N = 1,012). The bar chart shows the average number of correctly solved large matrixes (scale: 0-20). Error bars indicate standard error.Participants who were given the option to pre-commit ('optional pre-commit') or randomly assigned to a paternalistic policy condition ('forced pre-commit') performed significantly better at the behavioral effort task than participants who had to continuously choose between the non-incentivized small matrix and the incentivized large matrix in each trial ("no commitment") (p-values < .003 -.001, d-values = .22 -.60).

Figure 3 :

Figure3: Study 1 (N = 1,012). The bar chart shows the proportion of participants attempting to solve only the large matrixes (20/20 trials), some large matrixes (1-19/20 trials), or no large matrixes (0/20 trials) in each of the three conditions. All participants in all conditions were free to simply wait through each trial if they wanted to. Participants who were given the option to pre-commit to the incentivized high-effort option, or were forced to do so in a paternalistic policy condition, were significantly more likely to try to solve the maximum amount of 20 large matrixes (p < .001).

Figure 4 :

Figure 4: Study 2 (N = 1,010). The bar chart illustrates the proportion of participants who chose to pre-commit to the incentivized high-effort task at three different levels of trait self-control (Low: -1SD; Medium: average; High: +1SD). Error bars indicate standard error. Participants with medium and high self-control were significantly more likely to pre-commit to only solving high-effort trials than participants with low self-control (p < .001).
